notes.meaning: God began a new message to Moses about the autumn holy days. This separate introduction marks the start of the special appointments for the seventh month.

The first day of the seventh month was set apart as a day of rest and gathering, announced by the blast of horns. The loud sound woke the people from spiritual sleep, reminded them of God's law, and prepared them for the solemn day of repentance ten days later.
The people were told to put aside their daily jobs and bring fire offerings to the Lord. Setting aside regular work gave them time to worship and honor God on this holy day.

God gave Moses rules for the tenth day of the seventh month, called the Day of Atonement. Atonement means making peace with God and wiping away the guilt of sin. The people gathered to worship, brought sacrifices, and humbled themselves through fasting and sorrow for their sins.
No work of any kind was allowed on this day because atonement was being made before the Lord. Seeking God's forgiveness required a person's whole attention, leaving no room for worldly business.

Anyone who refused to humble themselves by fasting and repenting was cut off, meaning separated from God's people. Every person was guilty before God, so no one was allowed to treat this day with careless pride.
God warned that he would personally destroy anyone who did any work on this holy day. The complete ban on labor taught that people cannot add their own effort to the work of forgiveness.
God repeated that no work was permitted at all, making this a lasting rule for all future generations. Wherever the people lived, they were required to keep this holy day year after year.

This fast was kept as a complete Sabbath, lasting from sunset on the ninth day until sunset on the tenth day. Stopping their daily tasks before dark gave families time to prepare their hearts for the solemn fast.

God told Moses that the Feast of Tabernacles would start on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and last for seven days. A tabernacle is a temporary shelter or booth made of leafy branches. The feast reminded Israel of the shelters they lived in after escaping Egypt.
The opening day of the festival was a sacred assembly where all ordinary work stopped. This restful start allowed the people to focus on praising God together.

Offerings were burned on the altar on each of the seven days, followed by a sacred eighth day of rest and gathering. This eighth day closed the feast and the entire yearly festival cycle as families prepared to return to their homes.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that this eighth day corresponds to the great day of the feast mentioned in John 7:37.

notes.meaning: These verses sum up the appointed yearly festivals and their required offerings, such as burnt, grain, and drink sacrifices. These special feasts did not replace the regular weekly Sabbaths, nor did they take the place of personal gifts and voluntary offerings to God.

The feast took place after the people had gathered the final harvest of grapes, olives, and fruit from their land. Both the first day and the eighth day were observed with complete rest. It was a time to celebrate God's generous provision for their daily lives.

On the first day, the people gathered leafy branches from palm trees, willows, and other thick, healthy trees. Unlike the quiet fasting of the Day of Atonement, this festival called for seven days of open joy and praise before the Lord.

Israel was commanded to keep this seven-day festival every year as a permanent law. Celebrating it in the seventh month helped every generation remember God's goodness at the end of the agricultural year.
All native-born Israelites were commanded to move out of their houses and live in leafy booths for seven days. These simple huts were set up in open courtyards, streets, and flat rooftops.

Living in booths reminded future generations that God sheltered their ancestors when he delivered them from Egypt. Remembering their humble beginnings in the wilderness kept them from becoming proud or forgetting that their comfortable homes came from God.
Moses faithfully shared all of the Lord's commands about the sacred festivals with the people of Israel. He delivered God's calendar exactly as it had been revealed to him.
